metaDescription: Decode percent-encoded URL text such as %20 and %C3%AB back to readable characters, with an option to treat plus signs as spaces. Free, in your browser.
intro: Turn percent-encoded text like %3D, %20 and %C3%AB back into readable characters. An option lets you treat plus signs as spaces for query strings from HTML forms.
why:
Links copied from analytics, server logs and redirect chains are full of %2F and %3F, and you cannot tell where a nested URL begins and ends. A search query stored in a log is unreadable until it is decoded.

This tool reverses percent-encoding with the browser's decodeURIComponent, so multi-byte UTF-8 sequences become proper characters. One checkbox handles the form convention where + means a space, which the standard function leaves alone. If the text contains a broken sequence such as a lone %, you get a clear message. Nothing leaves your browser.
howTo: Paste the encoded text or URL into the box.
Tick "Treat + as space" if the text comes from an HTML form or a query string.
Read the decoded text in the output.
Copy the result, or fix the input if it reports malformed encoding.

faq.q: When should I treat + as a space?
faq.a: Use it for application/x-www-form-urlencoded data, which is what HTML forms and most query strings use. Leave it off for paths and for plain percent-encoded text, where a plus sign is a real plus sign.
A % is not followed by two hex digits, or the bytes do not form valid UTF-8. This happens with truncated links or text that was never encoded. Fix or remove the broken sequence and try again.

faq.q: My result still contains %25 or looks encoded. Why?
faq.a: The text was probably encoded twice. Run the decoder a second time on the output. %25 is an encoded percent sign, which is the usual sign of double encoding.

faq.q: Will it decode a whole URL?
faq.a: Yes, but it decodes everything, including characters that were escaped on purpose, such as %26 for an ampersand. To inspect the parts safely, use the URL Parser, which splits the address first.
